findings.title: The 'connection dead' warning is a reap of an already-dead socket, not a liveness verdict
findings.our_ref: src/networking/ibd.lisp:1591 (handle-peer-fin, log line at :1605), driven from drain-and-reap-peer at src/networking/ibd.lisp:1872; the only writers of connection-connected NIL are src/networking/connection.lisp:454 (send-queue flush error), :532 and :540 (send-bytes error), :645 (%abandon-receive: EOF, I/O error, or a give-up that had consumed bytes) and src/networking/v2-transport.lisp:167, :182, :191 (oversize packet, body read failed, Poly1305 auth failure)
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/net.cpp:2204-2218 (SocketHandlerConnected: recv()==0 or a send error sets fDisconnect), :709-713 (CNode::DisconnectMsg), and net.cpp:2008-2059 (InactivityCheck), all of which log at LogDebug(BCLog::NET)
findings.core_does: Core reports an ordinary peer hangup at LogDebug(BCLog::NET) with a reason attached to the line (recv()==0, socket send error, socket receive timeout, version handshake timeout), and it separates the socket-level reap from every rule that JUDGES a peer.
findings.we_do: handle-peer-fin logs 'Peer ~A connection dead - disconnecting' at WARN whenever (not (connection-connected conn)) is true, for a peer in ANY state, and calls disconnect-peer. It consults nothing else: no clock, no counter, no peer state. Every one of the seven writers above produces the identical line with no reason code, and each of our OWN liveness rules (check-peer-health, connection-receive-expired-p, retry-timed-out-requests, consider-peer-eviction) calls disconnect-peer directly and logs a different line, so it can never be the source of this one.
findings.impact: This is the explanation of the live observation: 50-70 of these lines an hour means 50-70 sockets an hour that the REMOTE closed (or that our write failed on), not 50-70 healthy peers we judged dead. The line is unactionable as logged - it cannot distinguish a peer that hung up from a v2 authentication failure from our own send error - and at WARN, ordinary peer turnover on a public node reads as a fault. The repetition of the SAME address is not this function's doing; it is the redial cadence in finding 33c6687d.
findings.executed: scripts/dev.sh eval: handle-peer-fin on three fabricated peers -> (:DEAD-CONN-REAPED T :STATE-AFTER :DISCONNECTED :CONN-AFTER NIL) for a :ready peer with connected NIL, (:NON-READY-ALSO-REAPED T) for a :handshaking one, (:ALIVE-REAPED NIL) for a connected one. Separately, a REAL loopback TCP peer driven through drain-and-reap-peer 50 times with nothing sent stayed (:STATE :READY :CONNECTED T :RECEIVE-IN-PROGRESS NIL :EXPIRED NIL) - the pump does not declare a quiet-but-alive peer dead.

findings.title: The outbound full-relay refill dials a start-up snapshot of addrman in fixed order, with no last-try cooldown
findings.our_ref: src/node/peers.lisp:805 (the dolist over (node-known-addresses node) inside replace-disconnected-peers, src/node/peers.lisp:744-848); node-known-addresses is assigned exactly once, at src/node/peers.lisp:541 in connect-to-peers, from max-peers*8 select-dialable-address picks
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/net.cpp:2790-2860 (ThreadOpenConnections: addrman.Select() per attempt at :2804-2822, the netgroup test at :2825-2827, and 'only consider very recently tried nodes after 30 failed attempts' -> 'if (current_time - addr_last_try < 10min && nTries < 30) continue;' at :2839-2841), with addrman's own GetChance (0.01x within 10 minutes of the last attempt, 0.66^n_attempts) and IsTerrible
findings.core_does: Core re-samples addrman on EVERY dial attempt, up to 100 tries per pass, and skips any candidate tried in the last 10 minutes unless it has already rejected 30 candidates. Selection is probabilistic and back-off weighted, so a peer that keeps failing is dialed exponentially less often and the candidate pool is the whole address book, including everything learned from addr gossip since start-up.
findings.we_do: replace-disconnected-peers walks node-known-addresses - a list sampled from addrman ONCE at start-up and never refreshed - in fixed order, dialing each unless it is already connected or its /16 is taken. There is no last-attempt cooldown, no GetChance weighting, no IsTerrible filter and no addrman Select() on this path at all (maintain-block-relay-peers is the only dialer that uses addrman on its own initiative, src/node/peers.lisp:1075). maintain-peers runs once per sync pass (src/node/init.lisp:1117), i.e. every ~30s at tip and sooner whenever headers arrive.
findings.impact: Two consequences. (1) Churn amplification: a peer that drops us is re-dialed from the head of the same list within ~30 seconds, forever - which is exactly the observed signature of the same addresses recurring 20+ times an hour. Core would not touch that address again for 10 minutes and would then pick it with probability 0.01 x 0.66^n. (2) Eclipse surface: the refill candidate space is frozen at max-peers*8 = 64 addresses captured at boot, so every address learned from addr gossip afterwards is unreachable to the full-relay refill. A node whose 64 boot candidates go stale cannot refill an outbound full-relay slot at all, while addrman holds thousands of usable entries.
findings.executed: scripts/dev.sh eval: %dial-outbound-peer stubbed to record and fail, five consecutive replace-disconnected-peers sweeps on a node with four known addresses and NO address book -> (:DIALS-IN-ORDER ("203.0.113.1" "198.51.100.7" "192.0.2.9" "10.9.0.4" x5) :DISTINCT 4 :TOTAL 20): the same four addresses, in the same order, 20 dials, with no cooldown - and the absent address book proves the path never consults addrman.

findings.title: One stall round disconnects a peer: the per-peer block-timeout budget is spent once per timed-out block
findings.our_ref: src/networking/ibd.lisp:1296-1300 (retry-timed-out-requests calls record-block-timeout once per timed-out HASH), src/networking/peer.lisp:1549 (record-block-timeout) and src/networking/peer.lisp:1465 (+max-block-timeouts+ = 15), src/networking/ibd.lisp:1217-1236 (compute-block-download-timeout: 90 + 5*(n-1)), src/networking/ibd.lisp:15-30 (+block-stalling-timeout+ = 30, +stalling-near-tip-margin+ = 144), src/networking/ibd.lisp:171 (max-in-flight = 16)
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp:6110-6122 (the block-download timeout: current_time > state.m_downloading_since + nPowTargetSpacing * (BLOCK_DOWNLOAD_TIMEOUT_BASE + BLOCK_DOWNLOAD_TIMEOUT_PER_PEER * nOtherPeersWithValidatedDownloads) -> fDisconnect), :148-150 (BASE = 1, PER_PEER = 0.5, against nPowTargetSpacing = 600s), :1223 and :1263 (m_downloading_since is re-stamped on each delivery, so the clock measures silence, not request age), :6096-6107 (the separate stalling-peer rule, 2s doubling to 64s, which fires only when the download window cannot move)
findings.core_does: Core disconnects a downloading peer when it has delivered NOTHING for nPowTargetSpacing * (1 + 0.5 * other_downloading_peers) - a floor of 600 seconds, 2700 seconds with eight downloading peers - measured from the last delivery, and it makes that decision once per peer, not once per block. The much shorter stalling timeout is a different rule that fires only when the whole download window is blocked and deliberately doubles (to 64s max) after each use so our own bandwidth cannot mass-evict peers.
findings.we_do: retry-timed-out-requests iterates every timed-out in-flight hash and calls record-block-timeout for each one, incrementing the same per-peer counter. A silent peer's in-flight blocks were all requested within the same pass, so they all expire in the same pass: the counter goes 0 -> 16 (the per-peer in-flight cap) in ONE call and crosses the 15 budget immediately. The timeout itself is 90 + 5*(n-1) seconds (125s with eight peers, one fifth of Core's floor) and drops to a flat 30 seconds whenever we are within 144 blocks of the header tip - i.e. in nearly every steady-state catch-up - or the block queue is saturated.
findings.impact: The +max-block-timeouts+ = 15 budget its own docstring says exists to 'tolerate a normal stalled batch without evicting peers who are simply mid-transit on big blocks' is consumed by a single stall round. The effective rule is: a peer holding a full 16-block window that delivers nothing for 125 seconds (or 30 seconds near the tip) is disconnected on the next retry pass. Honest peers on slow or lossy links, and every peer during a brief local pause, are dropped where Core would wait at least 600 seconds - and each drop is followed by an immediate redial of the same frozen candidate list (finding 33c6687d).
findings.executed: scripts/dev.sh eval: a fresh ibd-context with 16 in-flight blocks (the max-in-flight cap) all backdated 200s, one :ready peer, one call to retry-timed-out-requests -> (:PER-PEER-IN-FLIGHT-CAP 16 :MAX-BLOCK-TIMEOUTS-BUDGET 15 :TIMED-OUT-IN-ONE-PASS 16 :PEER-TIMEOUT-COUNT-AFTER 16 :PEER-STATE-AFTER :DISCONNECTED :ROUNDS-OF-SILENCE-NEEDED 1).

findings.title: Any error raised by a message handler disconnects the peer; Core catches every ProcessMessage exception
findings.our_ref: src/networking/ibd.lisp:1723-1738 (safely-dispatch-peer-message: a bare (error (c) ...) clause that logs and calls disconnect-peer), plus the outer (error (c) ...) clause in drain-and-reap-peer at src/networking/ibd.lisp:1840-1855; the handlers it wraps include src/networking/protocol.lisp:169 (ping) and :178 (pong), which read a u64 out of the payload unguarded
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp:5283-5287 (ProcessMessage's catch: 'Exception %s caught' at LogDebug, connection kept) and :4990-5048 (the PONG handler's explicit short-payload branch: nAvail < sizeof(nonce) sets sProblem = 'Short payload', cancels the outstanding ping, logs at LogDebug and does not disconnect)
findings.core_does: Core wraps every ProcessMessage call in try/catch: a deserialization failure - a truncated payload, a bad count, anything the handler throws - is logged at debug and the connection is KEPT. Punishment is only ever explicit (Misbehaving / fDisconnect at a named rule). PONG in particular has a hand-written branch for a short payload that treats it as another implementation's bug, cancels the ping and keeps the peer.
findings.we_do: safely-dispatch-peer-message catches every condition of type ERROR from the handler and disconnects the peer, logging 'sent a malformed/unprocessable ~A message'. There is no distinction between a protocol violation, a truncated payload Core tolerates, and a bug of our own inside the handler.
findings.impact: A single 24-byte message drops the connection. Concretely: a pong with a 0- or 4-byte nonce - the exact case Core names 'Short payload' and forgives - disconnects us, as do a short ping, a short feefilter and a short sendcmpct. More seriously, this converts ANY deserialization or logic bug in any of the 36 handlers into node-wide peer churn: the failure is per-peer but the trigger is usually per-message-type, so every peer that sends that message type is dropped, and the frozen candidate list (33c6687d) redials them within 30 seconds. Core's shape - forgive the exception, punish only at a named rule - exists precisely so that our own bugs cannot cost us the peer set.
findings.executed: scripts/dev.sh eval: handle-message plus safely-dispatch-peer-message over five short payloads -> pong/0 bytes, pong/4 bytes, ping/0 bytes, feefilter/3 bytes and sendcmpct/1 byte each raised SB-INT:INVALID-ARRAY-INDEX-ERROR and each left (:PEER-SURVIVES-DISPATCH NIL :STATE :DISCONNECTED).

findings.title: Height-based eviction has no Core counterpart and applies to inbound and manual peers alike
findings.our_ref: src/networking/peer.lisp:1565-1580 (consider-peer-eviction), driven every download cycle at src/networking/ibd.lisp:2166-2172
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp:5292-5350 (ConsiderEviction: gated on !m_chain_sync.m_protect && pto.IsOutboundOrBlockRelayConn() && state.fSyncStarted, and judged on pindexBestKnownBlock's CHAIN WORK, which UpdateBlockAvailability keeps current), :5352-5457 (EvictExtraOutboundPeers, outbound only), :5181-5190 (the NoBan and IsManualConn punishment exemptions); refs/bitcoin/src/net.h:771-785 (CNode::IsOutboundOrBlockRelayConn)
findings.core_does: Core has no height-based eviction at all. Every automatic disconnection rule it does have is restricted to outbound / block-relay connections (IsOutboundOrBlockRelayConn), exempts manual connections and NoBan peers, and is driven by the peer's CURRENT best-known block work, which UpdateBlockAvailability refreshes on every inv and headers message.
findings.we_do: consider-peer-eviction disconnects any peer that is :ready, advertised a non-negative height, and whose height is more than 1000 below ours. Its only guard is peer-state: inbound peers, operator-pinned -addnode / -connect peers and NoBan peers are all eligible. The number it compares is peer-start-height, which is the height in the peer's VERSION message and is frozen at handshake - our own sync-blockchain docstring (src/node/sync.lisp:23-26) says exactly that about the same slot - so a peer that has since caught up is judged on a stale number it can never update.
findings.impact: A node still in its own initial block download that connects to us inbound is disconnected on sight, every download cycle, and will keep re-dialing - a self-sustaining connect/disconnect loop we cause and cannot stop from our side. An -addnode peer that is behind is worse: connect-added-nodes redials every missing added node on the ~30s maintenance tick, so the operator's pinned peer is dropped and redialed in a loop indefinitely. The rule also never re-evaluates: peer-start-height is fixed for the life of the connection, so catching up cannot save the peer.
findings.executed: scripts/dev.sh eval: four peers with start-height 100 evaluated at our height 2000 -> (:INBOUND T :MANUAL T :OUTBOUND T :UNKNOWN-HEIGHT NIL :AT-1100 NIL). Inbound and manual peers are evicted exactly like an outbound one; only the -1 'unknown height' sentinel and a gap under 1000 are spared.

findings.title: record-misbehavior and ban-peer retire a peer without the disconnect hook, orphanage or headers-sync cleanup
findings.our_ref: src/networking/peer.lisp:1710-1718 (record-misbehavior's teardown) and src/networking/peer.lisp:1721-1733 (ban-peer), against src/networking/peer.lisp:458-483 (disconnect-peer) and the registration comment at src/networking/protocol.lisp:509-511 ('the tracker must observe every disconnect path')
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp FinalizeNode, reached from CConnman::DisconnectNode for every removal including MaybeDiscourageAndDisconnect (:5202-5206); it runs the tx-download manager's DisconnectedPeer, TxOrphanage::EraseForPeer and the Peer-state reset unconditionally
findings.core_does: Core has exactly one node-removal path. However a peer leaves - inactivity, misbehaviour, a ban, an eviction - FinalizeNode runs, so the tx-request tracker, the orphanage and the peer's sync state are always cleaned up together.
findings.we_do: record-misbehavior closes the connection, sets :disconnected and releases the outbound-protection slot, and stops there. It does not run *peer-disconnect-hook* (the tx-request tracker's DisconnectedPeer), does not call orphan-erase-for-peer, and does not clear peer-headers-sync - three of the four duties disconnect-peer performs. ban-peer is the same shape and additionally leaves the peer in state :banned, which replace-disconnected-peers does not reap.
findings.impact: The tracker's per-peer tables *tx-peer-announcements* and *tx-peer-in-flight* are keyed by the peer OBJECT and are only ever removed by the hook, so every misbehaving peer leaves a permanent entry that pins the whole peer struct for the life of the process. Its announcements survive until the 60-second expiry rather than being released at once, and its orphans sit in the orphanage until their own timer. The registration comment's claim that the tracker observes every disconnect path is false for two of the three paths. ban-peer has no caller in the tree today, so only the record-misbehavior half (seven call sites) is live.
findings.executed: scripts/dev.sh eval: with *peer-disconnect-hook* bound to a recorder, disconnect-peer / record-misbehavior / ban-peer on three peers -> (:DISCONNECT-HOOK-FIRED-FOR ("a") :STATES (:DISCONNECTED :DISCONNECTED :BANNED)). Only disconnect-peer fired the hook.

findings.title: record-misbehavior has no manual-connection exemption, so an -addnode peer is punished and redialed in a loop
findings.our_ref: src/networking/peer.lisp:1690-1698 (record-misbehavior's only exemption is +perm-noban+), with the redial at src/node/peers.lisp:995 (connect-added-nodes) and src/node/peers.lisp:985 (connect-specified-nodes), both driven from maintain-peers
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp:5181-5190 (MaybeDiscourageAndDisconnect: the NoBan exemption at :5181-5185 AND 'if (pnode.IsManualConn()) { LogWarning("Not punishing manually connected peer %d!"); return false; }' at :5187-5190)
findings.core_does: Core exempts manual connections from punishment independently of NoBan: an -addnode / -connect peer is never discouraged and never disconnected for bad behaviour, because the operator asked for it and Core redials it in a loop.
findings.we_do: record-misbehavior checks only the NoBan permission, which our peer-permission-flags derives from the address and direction, not from peer-manual. A manual peer that trips any of the seven misbehaviour sites is discouraged (so peer-discouraged-p makes it ineligible for inbound admission and for a fresh outbound dial at src/networking/peer.lisp:328) and disconnected.
findings.impact: An operator-pinned peer that trips a misbehaviour rule is dropped and added to the ephemeral discourage filter; connect-added-nodes then tries to redial it on every ~30s maintenance tick and connect-peer refuses because the address is discouraged, so the pinned peer silently stays down until the rolling filter forgets it - and comes back only to be punished again. The same rule also removes the one carve-out that lets an operator keep a peer whose implementation we disagree with, which is the whole point of -addnode.
findings.executed: Not separately executed; read from both trees. The exemption list in record-misbehavior is a single peer-has-permission-p test and peer-manual is never consulted anywhere in the function.

findings.title: A partially-received message is reaped after 300s; Core has no per-message stall rule at all
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/net.cpp:2041-2047 (InactivityCheck's only receive rule: now > last_recv + TIMEOUT_INTERVAL) and refs/bitcoin/src/net.h:59 (TIMEOUT_INTERVAL = 20min); CNode::vRecvMsg / Transport::ReceivedBytes hold a partial message indefinitely with no clock of their own
findings.core_does: Core keeps a partially-received message on the node for as long as the connection lives. It has no notion of a message that has taken too long; the only inactivity rule is 20 minutes without ANY received bytes, applied uniformly whether or not a message is in progress.
findings.we_do: Once any byte of a message has been CONSUMED, the peer must deliver more within 300 seconds or the pump disconnects it, measured from the last byte that arrived. A peer that has not started a message is exempt (correctly - the in-progress test is what keeps an idle poll from being read as a stall), so the rule is both stricter than Core where it applies and absent where Core's applies.
findings.impact: Four times stricter than the nearest Core rule, against a peer that is fully alive at the TCP level. A peer whose link stalls for five minutes mid-block - a Tor circuit rebuild, a congested path, a peer paused by its own backpressure - is dropped where Core would wait twenty minutes, and the drop is followed by an immediate redial of the same address (33c6687d). The complementary gap is that a peer which never starts a message is caught only by the 20-minute ping timeout, so we have no rule at all covering Core's last_recv case for a peer that answers pongs.
findings.executed: scripts/dev.sh eval on a real loopback TCP pair: the peer wrote 12 of the 24 header bytes and stopped -> (:IN-PROGRESS T :EXPIRED-NOW NIL :STATE :READY); backdating recv-last-progress to 299s -> NIL, to 301s -> T, and the next drain-and-reap-peer left (:STATE-AFTER-EXPIRED-DRAIN :DISCONNECTED).

findings.title: Core's InactivityCheck is absent and -peertimeout is bound to the handshake timeout instead
findings.our_ref: src/config-options.lisp:344-346 (-peertimeout mapped to *handshake-timeout-seconds*), src/config.lisp:302-310, src/networking/peer.lisp:1478-1490 (check-handshake-timeout, the only consumer), src/networking/connection.lisp:484-490 (connection-send-stalled-p, which additionally requires a non-empty send queue), and src/rpc/net.lisp:217-219 (the only readers of connection-last-recv-time / connection-last-send-time)
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/net.cpp:2003-2059 (ShouldRunInactivityChecks and InactivityCheck: the m_peer_connect_timeout grace period, the '!has_received || !has_sent' first-N-seconds rule, last_send + 20min, last_recv + 20min, and the handshake-not-completed rule), refs/bitcoin/src/net.h:87 (DEFAULT_PEER_CONNECT_TIMEOUT = 60) and refs/bitcoin/src/init.cpp:600 ('After connecting to a peer, wait this amount of time before considering disconnection based on inactivity')
findings.core_does: -peertimeout is the grace period before inactivity checks apply to a connection, and the window in which a peer that has never sent us anything (or that we have never sent anything to) is dropped. The four inactivity rules that follow it - send timeout, receive timeout, handshake-not-completed, never-spoke - are one function evaluated on every socket-handler pass.
findings.we_do: -peertimeout is parsed into *handshake-timeout-seconds*, whose only consumer is check-handshake-timeout for peers not yet :ready. There is no last_recv rule; there is no last_send rule independent of the send queue (connection-send-stalled-p requires plusp send-queue-bytes, so a connection whose socket has taken nothing for 20 minutes but has nothing queued is judged healthy); there is no '!has_received || !has_sent' rule. connection-last-recv-time and connection-last-send-time are maintained on every read and write and are read only by getpeerinfo.
findings.impact: Mostly benign in practice - the ping half of check-peer-health is a faithful port of MaybeSendPing (interval 120s, timeout 1200s, both measured from the last ping SENT) and catches the peer that stops answering, which is Core's real target. The residue is that an operator setting -peertimeout gets a different knob from the one Core documents (a handshake deadline, not an inactivity grace period), and that two accounting slots exist solely to be reported rather than enforced.
findings.executed: scripts/dev.sh eval on a real loopback TCP peer: check-peer-health returned (:NEVER-PINGED :PING-SENT) (:QUIET-119S :OK) (:QUIET-121S :PING-SENT) (:PING-OUTSTANDING-1199S :OK) (:PING-OUTSTANDING-1201S :DISCONNECT) (:SILENT-25MIN-BUT-ANSWERING-PINGS :OK :STILL-CONNECTED T) (:SEND-QUEUE-STALLED-21MIN :DISCONNECT) (:EMPTY-QUEUE-NOTHING-SENT-21MIN :OK) - the ping constants match Core exactly, and the last line is the send-side gap.

coverage_note: Survey only; nothing under src/ or tests/ was changed. Read both trees and executed seven probes in the project container (bitcoin-lisp-sbcl:2.6.5-4, warm image in this worktree). Covered: handle-peer-fin and the complete set of writers of connection-connected NIL (connection.lisp send/receive paths, v2-transport.lisp); drain-and-reap-peer's drain loop, send-pause gate, per-message and per-byte budgets and the half-read-message reaper; the resumable v1 and v2 readers and their EOF / give-up rules; receive-message / receive-message-blocking framing and their disconnect points (bad magic, oversized, incomplete payload, bad checksum kept); check-peer-health against Core MaybeSendPing and InactivityCheck; check-peers-health, maintain-peers, replace-disconnected-peers, connect-to-peers, maintain-block-relay-peers, connect-added-nodes / connect-specified-nodes and %dial-outbound-peer against ThreadOpenConnections; consider-chain-sync-eviction against ConsiderEviction and consider-peer-eviction (which has no Core counterpart); merge-inbound-peers and the inbound eviction pool against eviction.cpp; the block-download scheduler (compute-block-download-timeout, get-timed-out-requests, retry-timed-out-requests, release-orphaned-in-flight, request-blocks-from-peers backpressure and gap-only mode) against SendMessages' stalling / BLOCK_DOWNLOAD_TIMEOUT / headers-sync-timeout block; the block-relay handlers (ping, pong, sendheaders, feefilter, inv's block arm, headers, block, getheaders) and the misbehaviour / discourage / ban paths against MaybeDiscourageAndDisconnect and FinalizeNode; the handshake message order (version, wtxidrelay, sendaddrv2, sendtxrcncl, verack) and %await-verack against net_processing.cpp:3715-3744. Verified-clean and therefore NOT reported: the ping interval and timeout constants are Core's and the decisions match at both boundaries; the pump does not disconnect a quiet-but-alive peer (50 passes on a real socket); the post-verack disconnect rules for sendaddrv2 / wtxidrelay / sendtxrcncl are present and correctly placed; relay-transaction already refuses to announce to an fRelay=0 peer (which is what Core disconnects for) and handle-inv already implements Core's reject_tx_invs disconnect; the headers count is bounded at +max-headers-count+ by the parser; the chain-sync eviction port is faithful apart from Core's fSyncStarted gate, whose only divergence is during IBD where branch A clears anyway (judged too speculative to report without execution). NOT covered, with the dimension that inherits each: the tx-relay half of protocol.lisp - handle-tx, handle-notfound, the tx-request tracker, the inv trickle - was surveyed as dimension 4 and its eleven findings are not repeated here; cmpctblock / blocktxn / getblocktxn and the high-bandwidth peer set were excluded as just-fixed (exclusions.md) and only their timeout hook (check-compact-block-timeout) was read; BIP324 handshake cryptography and the v1/v2 detection sniff belong to the crypto dimension, not this one - only their connection-teardown effects were traced; addrman's bucket mathematics, Good/Attempt accounting and peers.dat serialization belong to the peer-addrman dimension (this survey only shows that the full-relay refill never calls into it); the inbound handshake running inline on the accept thread is in the GA1-GA9 exclusion list and was not re-reported; SOCKS5 / Tor control / I2P transports were not opened. Concurrency was not exercised: every probe ran on one thread, so races between the sync thread's pump, the inbound listener thread pushing to pending-inbound-peers, and RPC-thread disconnects (disconnectnode, setban) are untested here - and that is where the remaining risk in this seam sits, since node-peers is single-writer only by convention.
